failure_review.question: Which invariant can break?
failure_review.answer: A seat may be sold once, and a payment may be captured only for a booking that was actually ticketed. Both break at the same place: an ambiguous outcome from the airline or the PSP, where a timeout means the effect may or may not have happened and treating it as failure is exactly as wrong as treating it as success.

failure_review.question: Which metric detects it first?
failure_review.answer: The count of bookings sitting in an unresolved outcome state, and their age. Payment success rate and booking conversion both look normal while these accumulate, because an ambiguous booking has neither failed nor succeeded and therefore appears in neither number.

failure_review.question: How is the blast radius contained?
failure_review.answer: The search path and the booking path are separated so that a GDS quota exhaustion degrades search rather than stopping sales, holds expire on their own so an abandoned checkout returns inventory without intervention, and each external provider sits behind its own breaker and budget.

failure_review.question: Can retry duplicate or reorder work?
failure_review.answer: Yes at every external boundary, which is why the saga carries an idempotency key per step rather than per booking. A retried ticket issue must return the original ticket, and a retried capture must return the original capture — otherwise a customer is charged twice for one seat.

failure_review.question: How do we repair and prove recovery?
failure_review.answer: Resolve the unresolved set by querying each provider for the true outcome, then either complete or compensate — never by guessing from a local record. Recovery is proven when the unresolved-outcome count returns to zero, held inventory matches the airline’s view for a sampled set of flights, and no booking holds a capture without a ticket.

vi.title: Hệ thống OTA đặt vé máy bay
vi.excerpt: Thiết kế search, seat hold có expiry, payment và ticket issuance quanh hệ thống airline bên ngoài, outcome mơ hồ và policy overbooking có chủ đích.
vi.scope: Cho traveller tìm fare thay đổi liên tục, giữ inventory khan hiếm, trả tiền và nhận ticket/PNR qua một hay nhiều tích hợp GDS/airline. Giữ money-and-seat path đúng trong khi search nhanh, có cache và chấp nhận stale rõ ràng.
functional: Tìm itinerary và quote fare có expiry, source cùng snapshot baggage/rule rõ.
Tạo seat hold idempotent, hoàn tất payment và issue ticket qua booking workflow phục hồi được.
Release hold hết hạn, reconcile kết quả PSP/GDS mơ hồ và publish booking status cho client.
Hỗ trợ allocation overbooking hữu hạn theo policy, tách khỏi accidental double-selling.
quality: Không có hai confirmed booking dùng cùng physical seat trừ khi overbooking pool cho phép rõ.
Search có thể degrade sang cached availability nhưng confirmation không bao giờ coi cache là authoritative.
Kết quả từ external call: Mọi external call có timeout và idempotent khi có thể; unknown outcome đi vào reconciliation thay vì đoán.
Workflow expose pending state và sống qua restart service, queue hoặc orchestrator.
Timeout là outcome chưa biết, không phải failure — saga phải resolve bằng cách query provider với đúng client reference trước khi retry hay compensate.
capacity: Estimate search-to-book ratio, peak search QPS, concurrent hold, conversion và skew theo route/date.
Mô hình latency/quota GDS, freshness fare/availability, hold TTL và retry/reconnect storm.
Sizing booking path cho peak purchase và cô lập khỏi search workload lớn hơn nhiều.
Budget event retention, reconciliation backlog, payment/ticket timeout window và provider failover.

Hãy đặt con số cho hai đường riêng ra, vì chúng lệch nhau hai bậc: với tỷ lệ tìm-kiếm trên đặt-vé 100:1, một khối lượng đặt vé T3 cỡ 10k lượt/ngày nằm sau ~1 triệu lượt tìm/ngày, tức ~250 rps peak trên đường tìm kiếm so với ~2,5 rps peak trên đường đặt vé. Traffic du lịch là traffic tiêu dùng và dồn 10–20× quanh một đợt giảm giá vé hoặc một kỳ nghỉ.

Đánh giá cơ chế giữ chỗ theo từng tier: nên có ở T1 và T2, nơi tranh chấp hiếm và một lần đặt hụt chỉ là một lời xin lỗi; bắt buộc ở T3, vì hai khách cùng chạm tới ghế cuối trong khoảng một vòng gọi GDS là chuyện thường ngày chứ không phải trường hợp biên; cần scale riêng ở T4, nơi các lượt giữ chỗ, việc hết hạn của chúng và việc đối soát những lượt bị bỏ dở trở thành một thành phần có người sở hữu chứ không còn là một TTL trên một dòng dữ liệu.

Quota của GDS là một giới hạn cứng từ bên ngoài và thường chặn trước cả năng lực của chính bạn. Hãy size cache tìm kiếm ngược từ quota đó: nếu nhà cung cấp cho phép N lượt gọi mỗi giây thì chính tỷ lệ hit của cache quyết định tốc độ tìm kiếm bạn cung cấp được, chứ không phải số instance.
vi.diagram_title: Search path, hold authoritative và booking saga
data_model: Offer snapshot — itinerary, provider, fare/rule, availability observation, currency, version và expiry.
Seat hold — flight/seat hoặc inventory bucket, customer, quantity, status, fencing version và expires_at.
Booking saga — booking id, current step, provider reference, idempotency key, attempt và next action.
Payment ledger — debit/credit posting immutable, PSP reference và reconciliation state.
Ticket/PNR — provider locator, passenger, segment, issue status và provider state đã verify gần nhất.
Saga instance — saga_id, booking_id, saga_version, state, current_step và deadline_at; đây là process truth, tách khỏi booking row vốn là domain truth.
Saga step — (saga_id, step_name) kèm attempt, idempotency_key ổn định và unique toàn bảng, external_ref provider trả về, cùng compensation_status.

Outbox event — event_id, aggregate_type/id, aggregate_version tăng đơn điệu, event_type, schema_version và payload; unique trên (aggregate, version, type) để một write bị retry không phát cùng một fact hai lần.
Inbox message — (consumer_name, event_id) làm primary key; row này tồn tại chỉ để biến một event bị redeliver thành no-op ngay trong transaction của consumer.
API idempotency — (scope, idempotency_key) giữ request_hash và response đã lưu, để client retry nhận lại booking đầu tiên thay vì tạo booking thứ hai.
stack: Search/pricing stateless với Redis cache và circuit breaker/quota control riêng từng provider.
PostgreSQL/MySQL cho hold atomic, booking saga và payment ledger; conditional update hoặc row lock tại inventory boundary.
Kafka-compatible event bus + Outbox cho notification, analytics và availability projection.
Workflow/orchestrator durable cho hold → authorize/capture → issue, kèm worker expiry/reconciliation định kỳ.
WebSocket hoặc SSE cho realtime update hữu hạn; adapter GDS/airline và PSP sau anti-corruption layer.

Transactional outbox kèm CDC — service commit state và event trong cùng một local transaction, không gọi thẳng broker; Debezium đọc committed row từ WAL rồi route, đóng cửa sổ dual-write ở cả hai chiều.

Durable workflow engine cho orchestrator — booking chờ supplier callback, payment challenge và ticketing lâu hơn vòng đời một process, nên workflow state và timer phải sống sót qua crash chứ không nằm trong memory.
Schema registry kèm CI compatibility gate — một booking event có nhiều consumer độc lập, nên rename hoặc xoá field là sự cố lan rộng; thay đổi additive thì pass, breaking thì fail build.
tradeoffs: Một inventory authority atomic chặn accidental double-booking nhưng có thể phải partition theo flight/inventory bucket.
Hold TTL ngắn tăng utilization nhưng phạt payment chậm/accessibility flow; chỉ extend bằng policy rõ.
Orchestration làm money-and-ticket path dễ quan sát; choreography giảm coupling nhưng giấu một business transaction trong nhiều event.
Đặt bước khó reverse nhất cuối cùng, nhưng mọi timeout đều là unknown và phải query provider trước compensation.
Overbooking là commercial capacity model có limit/recovery cost, không phải race condition khoác áo eventual consistency.

Nhắm effectively-once về hiệu ứng nghiệp vụ, không nhắm exactly-once delivery — guarantee của broker dừng ở biên của chính nó, còn airline hay PSP nằm ngoài; idempotency key, unique constraint, inbox và reconciliation mới là thứ thật sự chặn lần charge thứ hai.

Compensation là một business state hợp lệ mới, không phải rollback nguyên trạng — khi seat đã hold, tiền đã authorize hoặc vé đã issue thì thế giới bên ngoài đã đổi, và forward recovery hoặc manual review đôi khi mới là đáp án đúng.

Orchestrate đường tiền-và-vé, choreograph mọi thứ phía sau — coordinator cho core flow timeout, compensation và saga_id auditable rõ ràng, còn notification, loyalty và analytics giữ loose coupling sau BookingConfirmed.
Giữ local transaction ngắn và không chứa remote call — mở database transaction xuyên suốt một call tới airline hay PSP đẩy thẳng tail latency của họ vào lock contention của mình.

code_samples.title: State machine của booking saga
code_samples.note: Mọi cạnh timeout đi vào OUTCOME_UNKNOWN thay vì thẳng tới failure, và MANUAL_REVIEW là một terminal state thật.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> VALIDATED
    VALIDATED --> INVENTORY_HELD
    INVENTORY_HELD --> PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> SUPPLIER_CONFIRMED
    SUPPLIER_CONFIRMED --> PAYMENT_CAPTURED
    PAYMENT_CAPTURED --> CONFIRMED

    VALIDATED --> FAILED
    INVENTORY_HELD --> COMPENSATING: unrecoverable failure
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> COMPENSATING: supplier failure
    SUPPLIER_CONFIRMED --> COMPENSATING: capture failure

    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> OUTCOME_UNKNOWN: timeout
    SUPPLIER_CONFIRMED --> OUTCOME_UNKNOWN: timeout
    OUTCOME_UNKNOWN --> SUPPLIER_CONFIRMED: lookup finds it
    OUTCOME_UNKNOWN --> COMPENSATING: lookup proves absence
    OUTCOME_UNKNOWN --> MANUAL_REVIEW: still ambiguous

    COMPENSATING --> COMPENSATED

    CREATED --> EXPIRED
    INVENTORY_HELD --> EXPIRED: hold deadline exceeded

    CONFIRMED --> [*]
    COMPENSATED --> [*]
    FAILED --> [*]
    EXPIRED --> [*]

code_samples.title: Saga, outbox và ba biên idempotency
code_samples.note: Client-to-API, saga-to-provider và broker-to-consumer mỗi biên cần key riêng; một bảng không phục vụ được cả ba.
code_samples.code:
-- Saga progress, outbox and the three idempotency boundaries.
-- Domain state and the event intent commit in ONE local transaction.

CREATE TABLE saga_instance (
    saga_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    booking_id    UUID NOT NULL,
    saga_version  INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- code version that started it
    state         TEXT NOT NULL,
    current_step  TEXT,
    deadline_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    version       BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,

    CHECK (state IN ('RUNNING', 'CONFIRMED', 'FAILED',
                     'COMPENSATING', 'COMPENSATED',
                     'MANUAL_REVIEW', 'EXPIRED'))
);

CREATE TABLE saga_step (
    saga_id             UUID NOT NULL,
    step_name           TEXT NOT NULL,
    attempt             INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status              TEXT NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key     TEXT NOT NULL,   -- stable across every retry
    external_ref        TEXT,            -- PNR, authorization_ref, hold_ref
    compensation_status TEXT,

    PRIMARY KEY (saga_id, step_name),
    UNIQUE (idempotency_key)
);

CREATE TABLE outbox_event (
    event_id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    aggregate_version BIGINT NOT NULL,   -- monotonic per aggregate
    event_type        TEXT NOT NULL,
    schema_version    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    payload           JSONB NOT NULL,
    occurred_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

    UNIQUE (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version, event_type)
);

CREATE TABLE inbox_message (
    consumer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    processed_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

    PRIMARY KEY (consumer_name, event_id)
);

CREATE TABLE api_idempotency (
    scope           TEXT NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL,
    request_hash    TEXT NOT NULL,   -- same key + different body = conflict
    resource_id     UUID,
    response_code   INTEGER,
    response_body   JSONB,

    PRIMARY KEY (scope, idempotency_key)
);

code_samples.title: Outbox producer — state và event trong một commit
code_samples.note: Không có publish trong request path. CDC chỉ đọc committed row, nên "đã commit mà không bao giờ publish" không thể xảy ra.
code_samples.code:
# Booking creation: domain row + event intent in one transaction.
# There is no producer.send() here - CDC reads committed rows only.

def create_booking(cmd, idempotency_key, db):
    with db.transaction() as tx:
        prior = tx.query_one(
            """SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body
                 FROM api_idempotency
                WHERE scope = 'create-booking' AND idempotency_key = %s
                  FOR UPDATE""",
            [idempotency_key])

        request_hash = canonical_hash(cmd)

        if prior:
            # Same key, different body is a client bug, not a retry.
            if prior.request_hash != request_hash:
                raise IdempotencyConflict()
            return prior.response_code, prior.response_body

        booking_id, saga_id = uuid4(), uuid4()

        tx.execute(
            """INSERT INTO booking (booking_id, saga_id, customer_id,
                                     status, currency, total_amount_minor)
               VALUES (%s, %s, %s, 'PENDING', %s, %s)""",
            [booking_id, saga_id, cmd.customer_id,
             cmd.currency, cmd.amount_minor])

        tx.execute(
            """INSERT INTO outbox_event (event_id, aggregate_type,
                    aggregate_id, aggregate_version, event_type,
                    schema_version, payload)
               VALUES (%s, 'booking', %s, 1, 'booking.created', 1, %s)""",
            [uuid4(), booking_id,
             json.dumps({'booking_id': str(booking_id),
                         'saga_id': str(saga_id), 'status': 'PENDING'})])

        response = {'booking_id': str(booking_id), 'status': 'PENDING'}

        tx.execute(
            """INSERT INTO api_idempotency (scope, idempotency_key,
                    request_hash, resource_id, response_code, response_body)
               VALUES ('create-booking', %s, %s, %s, 202, %s)""",
            [idempotency_key, request_hash, booking_id,
             json.dumps(response)])

    # Commit happened. Debezium will observe the outbox row from the WAL.
    return 202, response

code_samples.title: Inbox consumer — duplicate thành no-op
code_samples.note: Insert event id trước, ACK chỉ sau khi local commit, và guard aggregate version để một replay không kéo lùi state.
code_samples.code:
# The consumer side of at-least-once: duplicates must be no-ops.

def consume_booking_event(message, db):
    event = decode_and_validate(message)

    with db.transaction() as tx:
        inserted = tx.execute(
            """INSERT INTO inbox_message (consumer_name, event_id)
               VALUES (%s, %s) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING""",
            ['payment-service', event.event_id])

        if inserted.rowcount == 0:
            return ACK          # already applied in an earlier delivery

        current = tx.query_one(
            """SELECT version FROM payment_booking_view
                WHERE booking_id = %s FOR UPDATE""",
            [event.aggregate_id])

        if current:
            # Version guard: ordering is per-partition, not global.
            if event.aggregate_version <= current.version:
                return ACK                        # stale replay
            if event.aggregate_version > current.version + 1:
                raise SequenceGap(event.aggregate_id)   # park, do not apply

        apply_business_transition(tx, event)

        # A downstream event goes into THIS transaction's outbox, not a
        # separate publish - the same dual-write rule applies here.

    return ACK   # ACK only after the local commit succeeded

code_samples.title: Saga orchestration kèm compensation
code_samples.note: Compensation chạy theo thứ tự nghiệp vụ và dừng tại bước irreversible đầu tiên thay vì giả vờ có thể undo.
code_samples.code:
# Orchestrated booking saga. The durable workflow runtime owns retries,
# timers and resumption; every step below must still be idempotent.

async def run_booking_saga(ctx, booking):
    completed = []
    try:
        quote = await execute_step(ctx, name='REPRICE',
            action=lambda key: pricing.reprice(booking.quote_id,
                                               idempotency_key=key))
        completed.append(('REPRICE', quote))

        hold = await execute_step(ctx, name='HOLD_INVENTORY',
            action=lambda key: supplier.hold(booking.items,
                                             idempotency_key=key))
        completed.append(('HOLD_INVENTORY', hold))

        auth = await execute_step(ctx, name='AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT',
            action=lambda key: payment.authorize(booking.amount,
                                                 idempotency_key=key))
        completed.append(('AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT', auth))

        # Past this point a timeout means UNKNOWN, never "did not happen":
        # the resolver asks the supplier by client reference before any retry.
        confirmed = await execute_step(ctx, name='CONFIRM_SUPPLIER',
            action=lambda key: supplier.confirm(hold.ref,
                                                idempotency_key=key),
            ambiguous_outcome_resolver=supplier.lookup_by_client_ref)
        completed.append(('CONFIRM_SUPPLIER', confirmed))

        capture = await execute_step(ctx, name='CAPTURE_PAYMENT',
            action=lambda key: payment.capture(auth.ref,
                                               idempotency_key=key),
            ambiguous_outcome_resolver=payment.lookup)
        completed.append(('CAPTURE_PAYMENT', capture))

        await booking_service.confirm(booking.id)
        return 'CONFIRMED'

    except RetriableError:
        raise      # runtime backs off with jitter inside the deadline

    except UnrecoverableError as failure:
        return await compensate(ctx, booking, completed, failure)


async def compensate(ctx, booking, completed, failure):
    # Business order, not a blind reverse loop: some steps cannot be undone.
    for step, result in choose_compensation_order(completed):
        if step == 'CAPTURE_PAYMENT':
            await idempotent_retry(payment.refund, result.ref)

        elif step == 'CONFIRM_SUPPLIER':
            outcome = await idempotent_retry(supplier.cancel_if_allowed,
                                             result.ref)
            if outcome == 'NON_REFUNDABLE':
                # Forward recovery beats a rollback that cannot happen.
                return await manual_review(booking.id,
                                           reason='supplier_irreversible')

        elif step == 'AUTHORIZE_PAYMENT':
            await idempotent_retry(payment.void, result.ref)

        elif step == 'HOLD_INVENTORY':
            await idempotent_retry(supplier.release, result.ref)

    await booking_service.mark_compensated(booking.id, failure.code)
    return 'COMPENSATED'

failure_review.question: Invariant nào có thể vỡ?
failure_review.answer: Một ghế chỉ được bán một lần, và một khoản thanh toán chỉ được thu cho một booking đã thực sự xuất vé. Cả hai vỡ ở cùng một chỗ: một kết cục mơ hồ từ hãng bay hoặc từ PSP, nơi một lần timeout nghĩa là tác động có thể đã xảy ra hoặc chưa, và coi nó là thất bại thì sai đúng bằng coi nó là thành công.

failure_review.question: Metric nào phát hiện ra trước tiên?
failure_review.answer: Số booking đang nằm ở trạng thái kết cục chưa xác định, và tuổi của chúng. Tỷ lệ thanh toán thành công và tỷ lệ chuyển đổi đặt vé đều trông bình thường trong khi đám này tích tụ, vì một booking mơ hồ thì chưa hỏng mà cũng chưa xong nên không xuất hiện trong con số nào cả.

failure_review.question: Bán kính ảnh hưởng được chặn thế nào?
failure_review.answer: Đường tìm kiếm và đường đặt vé được tách ra để việc cạn quota GDS chỉ làm giảm chất lượng tìm kiếm chứ không dừng bán vé, các lượt giữ chỗ tự hết hạn nên một giỏ hàng bị bỏ dở trả lại tồn kho mà không cần can thiệp, và mỗi nhà cung cấp bên ngoài đều nằm sau breaker cùng ngân sách riêng của nó.

failure_review.question: Retry có thể nhân đôi hoặc đảo thứ tự công việc không?
failure_review.answer: Có, ở mọi ranh giới ra bên ngoài — đó là lý do saga mang idempotency key theo từng bước chứ không theo từng booking. Một lệnh xuất vé bị retry phải trả về đúng chiếc vé ban đầu, và một lệnh thu tiền bị retry phải trả về đúng lần thu ban đầu — nếu không khách bị trừ tiền hai lần cho một ghế.

failure_review.question: Sửa và chứng minh đã hồi phục thế nào?
failure_review.answer: Giải quyết tập chưa xác định bằng cách hỏi từng nhà cung cấp về kết cục thật, rồi hoặc hoàn tất hoặc bù trừ — không bao giờ bằng cách đoán từ một bản ghi cục bộ. Coi là hồi phục khi số kết cục chưa xác định về không, tồn kho đang giữ khớp với cách nhìn của hãng bay trên một tập chuyến bay lấy mẫu, và không booking nào giữ một khoản thu mà không có vé.

en.title: Booking and search platform at 1M requests a day
en.excerpt: Split a read-heavy search path from a correctness-critical booking path, using Kafka to make payment, notification and indexing asynchronous across sharded services.
en.scope: Serve roughly one million requests a day where the overwhelming majority are searches and only a small fraction become bookings. Raw throughput is not the question: 1M/day averages about 12 requests a second, so the peak-to-average ratio and two conflicting workloads determine the design. Keep search fast with bounded staleness; keep booking correct even when it is slower.
functional: Search read path: Search availability by date, location and filters, returning ranked results from an index rather than the transactional store.
Hold a specific unit for a bounded TTL so a user can complete checkout without another user taking it.
Confirm a booking through payment, then issue confirmation and release the hold atomically with respect to the order.
Expire abandoned holds and reconcile payments whose outcome is unknown, without operator intervention.
quality: No two confirmed bookings may consume the same unit; overselling is a correctness failure, not a capacity one.
Search may serve slightly stale availability, but the hold step always re-validates against the authoritative store.
A slow or failed payment provider must degrade booking latency, never search availability.
Every asynchronous consumer is idempotent: Kafka gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are normal traffic.
capacity: Peak traffic: 1M requests/day is about 12 rps average; size for the peak instead — a 10-20x daily peak puts the search path near 150-250 rps.
Booking write rate: Assume a 100:1 search-to-booking ratio: roughly 10k bookings/day, about 2-5 writes per second at peak on the correctness path.
Serialization boundary: Search is cacheable and horizontally scalable; the inventory write path is the only component that must serialize per unit.
Event retention: Size Kafka for booking events plus retries and replay: modest volume, but retention must cover a full reconciliation window.

Judge each component per tier rather than adopting the split wholesale: the read/write path separation is not needed at T1, worth it at T2, and mandatory at T3 where the search load would otherwise size the database that must serialize bookings; the Kafka hop is not needed at T1 and T2, worth it at T3 to keep payment and indexing off the request, and needs its own scaling story at T4 alongside partition count, consumer lag and replay.
en.diagram_title: Read path, authoritative write path and the Kafka fan-out
data_model: Inventory unit — the authoritative row, sharded by resource id so contention for one unit stays inside one shard.
Hold — unit id, user, expiry timestamp and state; the uniqueness constraint that prevents double-selling lives here.
Order — the booking aggregate with an idempotency key, its payment reference and an explicit state machine.
Search document — a denormalized, eventually consistent projection rebuilt from events, never read during confirmation.
Outbox — booking state changes written in the same transaction as the order and relayed to Kafka at least once with stable event ids; consumers deduplicate effects.
stack: API gateway plus separately deployed search and booking services, so the two scale on their own traffic shape.
Distributed SQL (CockroachDB, TiDB, Yugabyte) or a sharded relational store: booking needs real transactions, so range-sharding by resource keeps them single-shard.
Kafka as the event backbone — partition by booking or resource id so events for one entity keep their order.
A search index (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) plus a cache for hot queries, both fed asynchronously from Kafka.
The transactional-outbox pattern rather than dual writes: a database commit and a Kafka publish cannot be made atomic.
tradeoffs: At this volume a single well-indexed relational primary would likely cope. Sharding and microservices are being bought for isolation and independent deployment, not for throughput — say so rather than justifying them with the request count.

Kafka moves payment and notification off the request path, but converts booking into an asynchronous workflow: the user now sees a pending state, and every consumer needs idempotency and a dead-letter path.
A distributed database removes the single-primary ceiling and adds cross-shard latency; the design only pays off because bookings for one unit stay within one shard.
Holds trade inventory utilization for user experience: a long TTL blocks real demand, a short one loses checkouts under slow payments.
Failure review: the highest-risk paths are a payment whose result is unknown, a consumer replaying old events after a rollback, and index lag making search advertise units that are already gone.

code_samples.title: The one line that must serialize
code_samples.note: Everything else in this design scales horizontally. This statement is the serialization boundary, and the WHERE clause is what makes it safe without holding a lock across the request.
code_samples.code:
-- conditional decrement: the row is only updated if inventory is actually there,
-- so two concurrent bookings cannot both succeed on the last unit
UPDATE inventory
   SET available = available - :qty,
       version   = version + 1
 WHERE unit_id  = :unit_id
   AND available >= :qty;

-- zero rows updated means sold out — that is the answer, not an error to retry.
-- Reading the balance first and then updating is the race this replaces.

failure_review.question: Which invariant can break?
failure_review.answer: A unit of inventory may be booked at most once, and a booking that a customer was shown as confirmed must exist downstream. The first is protected by the conditional decrement; the second by publishing the event in the same transaction as the booking rather than after it.

failure_review.question: Which metric detects it first?
failure_review.answer: Consumer lag on the booking topic, read beside booking confirmation latency. A search-path incident is visible immediately, but a broken write path shows first as lag: bookings still succeed while payment, notification and indexing fall behind them.

failure_review.question: How is the blast radius contained?
failure_review.answer: Search is cacheable and horizontally scalable, so its failure never reaches the booking path. The only serializing component is the inventory row, and everything downstream of the booking is asynchronous, so a payment or indexing outage delays follow-up rather than blocking a sale.

failure_review.question: Can retry duplicate or reorder work?
failure_review.answer: Yes. A retried booking request must be deduplicated by an idempotency key or the conditional decrement runs twice and sells two units to one customer. Consumers are at-least-once, so payment and notification must both be idempotent on the booking id.

failure_review.question: How do we repair and prove recovery?
failure_review.answer: Replay the booking topic from the last committed offset; the inventory table is the source of truth and never needs reconstructing. Recovery is proven when consumer lag returns to baseline, a sampled set of bookings has exactly one payment and one notification each, and the search index matches the booking table for the affected window.

vi.title: Booking & search platform ở mức 1M requests/day
vi.excerpt: Tách high-read search path khỏi correctness-sensitive booking path, dùng Kafka để đưa payment, notification và indexing sang async giữa các service đã shard.
vi.scope: Phục vụ khoảng 1M requests/day, phần lớn là search và chỉ một phần nhỏ trở thành booking. Raw throughput không phải câu hỏi chính: 1M/day average chỉ khoảng 12 requests/s, nên peak/average ratio và hai workload trái ngược mới quyết định design. Search phải nhanh với staleness có giới hạn; booking phải đúng dù chậm hơn.
functional: Search read path: Search theo ngày, địa điểm và filter, trả ranked result từ index chứ không từ transactional store.
Resource hold: Giữ một unit cụ thể trong TTL giới hạn để user kịp checkout mà không bị người khác lấy mất.
Booking confirmation: Xác nhận booking qua payment, sau đó phát confirmation và release hold nhất quán với order.
Expiry & reconciliation: Tự động expire hold bị bỏ dở và reconcile payment outcome chưa rõ mà không cần manual intervention.
quality: No oversell: Không bao giờ có hai confirmed booking cùng chiếm một unit; oversell là correctness failure, không phải capacity failure.
Bounded staleness: Search được phép trả inventory hơi cũ, nhưng hold luôn revalidate với authoritative store.
Failure isolation: Payment chậm hoặc lỗi chỉ làm booking chậm, không được ảnh hưởng search availability.
Async idempotency: Mọi consumer đều idempotent; Kafka giao at-least-once nên duplicate record là bình thường.
capacity: Peak traffic: 1M requests/day ≈ 12 rps average; hãy size theo peak — peak factor 10–20× đưa search path lên khoảng 150–250 rps.
Booking write rate: Với search/booking ratio 100:1, khoảng 10k booking/day, tức khoảng 2–5 writes/s trên correctness-sensitive path.
Serialization boundary: Search cache được và scale ngang dễ; inventory write path là component duy nhất phải serialize theo từng unit.
Event retention: Tính Kafka capacity cho booking events cộng retry và replay; traffic vừa phải nhưng retention phải phủ trọn một reconciliation cycle.

Hãy đánh giá từng thành phần theo tier thay vì bê nguyên cả cách chia: việc tách đường đọc khỏi đường ghi không cần ở T1, nên có ở T2, và bắt buộc ở T3 — nơi nếu không tách thì tải tìm kiếm sẽ quyết định kích thước của chính cái database phải tuần tự hoá việc đặt chỗ; chặng Kafka không cần ở T1 và T2, nên có ở T3 để đẩy thanh toán và lập chỉ mục ra khỏi request, và cần scale riêng ở T4 cùng với số partition, độ trễ consumer và khả năng phát lại.
vi.diagram_title: Search read path, authoritative write path và Kafka fan-out
data_model: Inventory unit — authoritative record, shard theo resource id để contention trên một unit nằm gọn trong một shard.
Hold — unit id, user, expiry time và state; unique constraint chống bán trùng nằm ở đây.
Order — aggregate của booking kèm idempotency key, tham chiếu payment và một state machine tường minh.
Search document — bản chiếu denormalized, eventual consistency, dựng lại từ event và không bao giờ được đọc lúc xác nhận.
Outbox — thay đổi trạng thái booking ghi cùng transaction với order rồi relay sang Kafka at-least-once bằng stable event id; consumer deduplicate effect.
stack: API gateway cùng search service và booking service triển khai tách biệt, để mỗi bên scale theo workload shape của chính nó.
Distributed SQL (CockroachDB, TiDB, Yugabyte) hoặc relational store đã shard: booking cần transaction thật, nên shard theo range của resource giúp transaction nằm trong một shard.
Kafka làm xương sống event — partition theo booking id hoặc resource id để event của cùng một thực thể giữ đúng thứ tự.
Một search index (Elasticsearch hoặc OpenSearch) cộng cache cho truy vấn nóng, cả hai được nạp async từ Kafka.
Dùng transactional outbox thay vì dual write: commit database và publish Kafka không thể nguyên tử cùng nhau.
tradeoffs: Ở scale này, một relational primary đánh index tốt nhiều khả năng vẫn kham được. Sharding và microservice được mua để lấy isolation và khả năng deploy độc lập, không phải để lấy throughput — hãy nói thẳng điều đó thay vì lấy số request ra biện minh.
Kafka đưa payment và notification ra khỏi request path, nhưng biến booking thành async flow: user bắt đầu thấy trạng thái pending, và mọi consumer đều cần idempotency cùng dead-letter.
Distributed database gỡ bỏ trần của một primary duy nhất nhưng thêm cross-shard latency; design chỉ có lãi vì booking của cùng một unit luôn nằm trong một shard.
Hold là trade-off giữa inventory utilization và user experience: TTL dài chặn mất nhu cầu thật, TTL ngắn làm mất đơn khi payment chậm.
Review lỗi: rủi ro cao nhất là payment không rõ kết quả, consumer replay lại event cũ sau khi rollback, và index trễ khiến search quảng cáo những đơn vị đã hết.

code_samples.title: Dòng duy nhất buộc phải tuần tự
code_samples.note: Mọi thứ khác trong thiết kế này đều scale ngang được. Câu lệnh này là ranh giới tuần tự hoá, và mệnh đề WHERE là thứ khiến nó an toàn mà không phải giữ lock suốt cả request.
code_samples.code:
-- trừ có điều kiện: dòng chỉ được cập nhật nếu tồn kho thực sự còn,
-- nên hai lệnh đặt song song không thể cùng thành công trên đơn vị cuối cùng
UPDATE inventory
   SET available = available - :qty,
       version   = version + 1
 WHERE unit_id  = :unit_id
   AND available >= :qty;

-- không dòng nào được cập nhật nghĩa là đã hết hàng — đó là câu trả lời, không phải
-- một lỗi để retry. Đọc số lượng trước rồi mới update chính là cuộc đua mà cách này thay thế.

failure_review.question: Invariant nào có thể vỡ?
failure_review.answer: Một đơn vị tồn kho chỉ được đặt nhiều nhất một lần, và một booking mà khách đã được thấy là đã xác nhận thì phải tồn tại ở phía dưới. Cái thứ nhất được bảo vệ bằng lệnh trừ có điều kiện; cái thứ hai bằng cách phát event trong cùng transaction với booking chứ không phải sau nó.

failure_review.question: Metric nào phát hiện ra trước tiên?
failure_review.answer: Độ trễ consumer trên topic booking, đọc cạnh độ trễ xác nhận booking. Một sự cố ở đường tìm kiếm thì thấy ngay, nhưng một đường ghi hỏng lộ ra trước tiên bằng độ trễ: booking vẫn thành công trong khi thanh toán, thông báo và lập chỉ mục tụt lại phía sau.

failure_review.question: Bán kính ảnh hưởng được chặn thế nào?
failure_review.answer: Tìm kiếm thì cache được và scale ngang được, nên việc nó hỏng không bao giờ chạm tới đường đặt chỗ. Thành phần duy nhất phải tuần tự là dòng tồn kho, và mọi thứ nằm sau booking đều bất đồng bộ, nên một sự cố thanh toán hay lập chỉ mục chỉ làm chậm khâu hậu kỳ chứ không chặn một lần bán.

failure_review.question: Retry có thể nhân đôi hoặc đảo thứ tự công việc không?
failure_review.answer: Có. Một request đặt chỗ bị retry phải được khử trùng lặp bằng idempotency key, nếu không lệnh trừ có điều kiện chạy hai lần và bán hai đơn vị cho một khách. Consumer là at-least-once, nên thanh toán và thông báo đều phải idempotent theo booking id.

failure_review.question: Sửa và chứng minh đã hồi phục thế nào?
failure_review.answer: Phát lại topic booking từ offset đã commit cuối cùng; bảng tồn kho là nguồn sự thật và không bao giờ cần dựng lại. Coi là hồi phục khi độ trễ consumer về mốc nền, một tập booking lấy mẫu mỗi cái có đúng một lần thanh toán và một lần thông báo, và chỉ mục tìm kiếm khớp với bảng booking trong khoảng thời gian bị ảnh hưởng.

en.title: E-commerce at 1M, 10M and 100M requests/day: evolving Saga + Outbox by evidence
en.excerpt: Turn a concrete e-commerce Saga + Outbox architecture into an evolution plan: preserve stock and payment correctness while search, cart, checkout, eventing and storage scale only when their own signals demand it.
en.scope: Use the supplied e-commerce diagram as a logical target for a promotion: CDN and gateway at the edge; isolated search and cart paths; a durable Checkout Saga coordinating order, inventory and payment; and a local outbox beside each authoritative database. The image says 1M DAU and a 10x campaign, whereas this blueprint's shared yardstick is requests/day. Convert DAU into endpoint traffic before sizing anything, then decide what is one deploy at 1M requests/day, what splits at the 10M waypoint, and what only becomes justified near 100M or under an explicit blast-radius target. The skill is preserving the same business invariants while refusing distribution that has no measured constraint to remove.
functional: Browse and search: Serve product images from the CDN, product details from cache or the catalog, and ranked results from a rebuildable search projection whose stock may be stale.
Cart: Persist the cart durably while using Redis only to accelerate active carts; an eviction or Redis outage must not erase a customer's order intent.
Checkout: Accept one idempotent checkout command, persist Saga state, create the order, reserve stock, process payment, then confirm or compensate each participant through explicit transitions.
After payment: Fan `PaymentCompleted` out to reviews, notification, analytics and search/index updates without placing those consumers on the checkout latency path.
Recovery: Expire abandoned reservations, reconcile `UNKNOWN` payments against the provider, replay outboxes, quarantine poison events and redrive the DLQ only after the consumer defect is fixed.
quality: Stock invariant: Available stock never becomes negative, and at most one live reservation may consume the same scarce unit/version; search is not an authority for that decision.
Payment invariant: A client, gateway, Saga retry and provider webhook may all duplicate work, but one checkout intent can produce at most one captured amount under one provider idempotency key.
Local atomicity: Each service commits its state transition and outbox record in one local transaction; delivery and consumption remain duplicate-tolerant.
Failure isolation: Search, cart, payment and after-payment work use separate pools and bounded queues, so a slow PSP or review consumer cannot exhaust checkout or browse capacity.
Operability: Alert on aged Saga states, outbox age, consumer lag, DLQ growth, reserve conflicts, payment `UNKNOWN` age and reconciliation mismatches rather than CPU alone.
capacity: Unit guard: 1M DAU is not requests/day. Estimate `requests/day = DAU × journeys/user/day × API calls/journey`, then split by browse, cart and checkout endpoint; report the assumptions beside the result.

1M request scale: 1M requests/day is 11.6 rps average and about 250 rps peak under the site's 20x planning factor. One relational primary and one coarse application deployment may still be enough; preserve the logical ownership shown in the image without paying for a database and on-call team per box.

10M waypoint: 10M requests/day is 116 rps average and about 2,500 rps peak. A 10x promotion is a burst profile, not automatically 10M/day: measure its duration, endpoint mix, cache-hit ratio and hot-SKU skew, then cap accepted checkout work to the inventory and PSP drain rates.

Write amplification: One accepted checkout can create order, reservation and payment writes plus several outbox, inbox and derived-index records. Size database IOPS, WAL, broker ingress and consumers from commands and events per checkout, not from the public API count alone.

Serialized hot key: Ten stateless inventory replicas do not raise the safe rate for one SKU row or one ordered partition. Benchmark that critical section, reserve headroom, and use per-SKU admission or a waiting room when demand exceeds its drain rate.

100M scale: About 25,000 rps peak is a fleet-sizing number. Introduce shards or cells only for measured write/data volume, restore-time or blast-radius limits; model it as roughly ten independently operable T3-to-waypoint cells rather than one giant shared checkout.
en.diagram_title: Critical checkout commands, local outboxes and asynchronous effects
data_model: Product and search document — Product DB is authoritative for catalog data; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch is a denormalized projection with `source_version` and `indexed_at`, so it can be stale, discarded and rebuilt.
Cart — Durable cart rows own product, quantity and price-snapshot references; Cart Redis is a TTL acceleration tier for active sessions, never the only copy of checkout intent.

Checkout request and Saga — `idempotency_key`, canonical request hash, original response, Saga state, step attempts, deadlines and version. Keep request dedupe with the transaction that creates the Saga, not in an eventually consistent global cache.
Order — One aggregate with legal `CREATED → CONFIRMED | CANCELLED` transitions and a version. Order Service alone changes it; the Saga requests transitions but never writes Order DB directly.

Inventory reservation — `sku_id`, quantity, order id, expiry, state and fencing version. A conditional update or uniqueness constraint is the final oversell guard; Redis may protect capacity but not replace this invariant.

Payment attempt — Amount, currency, order id, provider idempotency key/reference and explicit `PENDING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED | UNKNOWN | REFUNDED` states. Timeout means query and reconcile, not retry with a new key.

Outbox and inbox — Stable event/command id, aggregate id, aggregate version, type, payload and occurred time. Outbox closes the database/broker dual-write gap; inbox or an effect-specific unique key makes at-least-once delivery harmless.
stack: Image CDN — Problem solved: remove large immutable image and static-file reads from application compute and origin bandwidth. Flow position: App/Web requests a content-addressed URL such as `products/42/sha256.webp` directly from the nearest edge; business APIs still enter the gateway. Failure / cost: a bad cache key serves stale content, an expiry wave stampedes the origin, and public caching can leak private responses; use versioned URLs, long immutable TTLs, origin shielding and a placeholder when the CDN is unavailable. Tier verdict: 1M worth it; 10M mandatory for image-heavy browse; 100M needs its own scaling story across regions and origins.

API Gateway — Problem solved: give clients one stable edge contract for TLS termination, authentication hand-off, coarse authorization, routing, request-size limits and per-route rate limits. Flow position: every dynamic `/search`, `/cart` and `/checkout` call enters here, receives a correlation id and is routed to an independently budgeted backend pool. Failure / cost: it is a high-blast-radius choke point; policy mistakes reject all traffic, retries can amplify overload, and deep business authorization here becomes unmaintainable. Run multiple instances across zones, fail closed for auth, return explicit `429` with backoff, and keep domain checks in services. Tier verdict: 1M worth it; 10M mandatory; 100M needs its own scaling story per cell or region.

Service discovery with Kubernetes Service/DNS — Problem solved: let gateway and services call a stable name while Pods and IPs are replaced. Flow position: `checkout.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to a Service whose EndpointSlices track healthy checkout replicas; clients still need connection timeouts, load balancing and readiness because DNS only finds an endpoint. Failure / cost: stale DNS caches, an unhealthy readiness probe or a control-plane outage can route poorly, while a second custom registry duplicates platform state. Tier verdict: platform discovery is 1M worth it and 10M mandatory once replicas move; a custom registry is not needed at either tier; 100M cross-cell discovery needs its own scaling story.

Search Service plus Elasticsearch/OpenSearch — Problem solved: full-text relevance, typo tolerance, filtering, faceting and sorting that a transactional Product DB should not execute on every browse request. Flow position: product and stock events update a versioned `products-v42` projection; Search Service queries it and returns `source_version` or `indexed_at`, while checkout revalidates stock in Inventory. Failure / cost: refresh and consumer lag make results stale, mappings and shard counts are expensive to change, hot queries exhaust heap, and out-of-order events can overwrite newer documents; reject older source versions and keep a rebuild path from Product DB/outbox. Tier verdict: 1M worth it when product search is real; 10M mandatory for the depicted search-heavy lane; 100M needs its own scaling story for shards, indexing and relevance.

Product Redis cache — Problem solved: absorb repeated product-detail reads and protect Product DB connection/IO budgets. Flow position: Search or Product Service performs cache-aside `GET product:{id}:v{source_version}`, loads the authoritative row on a miss, then `SET`s a bounded TTL; writes commit to Product DB first and invalidate or advance the versioned key. Failure / cost: stale values, eviction and Redis outage are expected; simultaneous misses create a stampede and one hot key can saturate a shard, so use single-flight fill, jittered TTL, negative caching with a short TTL and a direct-to-origin concurrency cap. Tier verdict: 1M worth it; 10M mandatory for the hot catalogue path shown; 100M needs its own scaling story for memory, hot keys and failover.

Cart DB plus Cart Redis — Problem solved: Cart DB preserves customer intent across sessions, while Redis reduces latency for repeatedly edited active carts. Flow position: Cart Service writes the durable cart with an optimistic version and may cache `cart:{customer_id}`; checkout always reloads or validates the durable version and current price/stock rules. Failure / cost: cache eviction must become a miss, never an empty cart; dual writes can diverge, long TTLs expose stale quantity and a hot anonymous campaign can consume memory. Prefer database-first plus invalidate, measure hit rate and cap cart size. Tier verdict: durable Cart DB is 1M mandatory; Cart Redis is 1M not needed, 10M worth it, and 100M needs its own scaling story.

Checkout Saga plus Checkout DB — Problem solved: preserve progress across the Order, Inventory and Payment transaction boundaries when no single ACID commit covers them. Flow position: Checkout persists `RECEIVED → STOCK_HELD → PAYMENT_PENDING → CONFIRMED`, deadlines and step attempts before issuing idempotent participant commands; workers can restart from durable state and compensations are explicit new commands. Failure / cost: the orchestrator couples workflow knowledge, can become a control-plane hotspot, and compensation may fail or be semantically impossible after an external effect. Partition workers by checkout/order id, fence concurrent transitions and reconcile aged non-terminal rows. Tier verdict: 1M not needed while all participants share one local transaction; 10M mandatory only after they become separate authorities; 100M needs its own scaling story per cell.

Idempotency store — Problem solved: make client retries, gateway retries and duplicate submissions return one logical checkout outcome. Flow position: the transaction that creates the Saga inserts `(tenant, idempotency_key, canonical_request_hash, status, original_response)` under a unique constraint; the same key with a different hash is rejected, while an exact replay returns the stored response. Failure / cost: a remote eventually consistent cache allows races, unbounded retention grows forever, and deleting keys too early reopens duplicate capture risk. Co-locate it with Checkout DB, define retention from the longest retry/webhook window and monitor hot keys. Tier verdict: 1M mandatory; 10M mandatory; 100M needs its own scaling story for partitioning and retention.

Order Service plus relational Order DB — Problem solved: own the legal order lifecycle and audit trail independently of the Saga's opinion. Flow position: idempotent `Create`, `Confirm` and `Cancel` commands perform conditional transitions such as `CREATED → CONFIRMED | CANCELLED`, then record an outbox event in the same transaction; no other service writes Order tables. Failure / cost: cross-service joins disappear, stale commands conflict by version, and premature service/database separation adds network and on-call cost. Keep indexes around customer/status/time and archive by policy rather than sharding the headline. Tier verdict: the relational state machine is 1M mandatory; a separate service/database is 1M not needed, 10M worth it for ownership/isolation, and 100M needs its own scaling story.

Inventory Service plus relational Inventory DB — Problem solved: make stock reservation the single authority that prevents oversell. Flow position: `Reserve(sku, qty, order)` performs one short conditional update such as `available >= qty AND version = expected`, inserts an expiring reservation and outbox row, then `Confirm` or `Release` transitions that exact reservation idempotently. Failure / cost: one promotional SKU remains a serialized hot key even with many replicas; lock waits, expired holds and duplicate release commands must be visible. Use a database constraint as the final guard, admission/waiting-room controls for the hot SKU and reconciliation for leaked reservations. Tier verdict: the invariant is 1M mandatory and 10M mandatory; 100M needs its own scaling story by SKU/warehouse, not random request sharding.

Payment Service plus relational Payment DB — Problem solved: isolate provider-specific APIs while keeping one authoritative payment-attempt ledger. Flow position: it stores amount, currency, order id, provider reference and one reused provider idempotency key, calls the PSP outside the database transaction, records webhook/status-query evidence, and emits a local outbox event. Failure / cost: timeout means `UNKNOWN`, not failed; retrying with a fresh key may double-charge, late success may require refund, and a slow PSP can exhaust checkout workers. Use strict timeouts, a separate concurrency budget, status polling/webhooks and financial reconciliation. Tier verdict: durable attempts and idempotency are 1M mandatory; provider isolation is 10M worth it; 100M needs its own scaling story per provider/region.

Transactional Outbox, relay and consumer Inbox — Problem solved: close the database/broker dual-write gap without a distributed transaction. Flow position: each Order, Inventory or Payment transaction appends a stable event id and aggregate version locally; a relay publishes unprocessed rows, and each consumer records the event id plus its side effect in one local transaction. Failure / cost: a relay crash after publish causes duplicates, backlog grows the source DB, and out-of-order delivery can apply stale state; therefore publication is at-least-once, not end-to-end exactly-once. Monitor oldest outbox age, batch with `SKIP LOCKED`, deduplicate and reject stale versions. Tier verdict: 1M not needed while one local transaction has no broker side effect; 10M mandatory for the depicted split; 100M needs its own scaling story for relay throughput and retention.

Kafka event log — Problem solved: retain replayable domain events and let checkout, search, analytics and after-payment consumer groups advance independently. Flow position: outbox relays publish `OrderCreated`, `StockReserved` and `PaymentCompleted` keyed by the aggregate whose order matters; one partition preserves order for that key and each group gets its own copy. Failure / cost: consumers can replay duplicates, rebalances pause work, retention can remove repair history, and adding partitions changes key distribution while one hot key still cannot use several partitions. Size partitions from measured bytes/events, use schemas and compatibility checks, and alert on oldest lag rather than broker CPU alone. Tier verdict: 1M worth it when replay or multiple groups are required; 10M mandatory for the pictured fan-out; 100M needs its own scaling story for partitions, storage and cross-cell replication.

RabbitMQ work queues — Problem solved: route one command or task to one logical worker with broker-side acknowledgements, redelivery and queue-level policies. Flow position: it can carry fulfilment, email or compensation commands whose consumer acknowledges only after its local effect commits; publisher confirms cover broker acceptance, not consumer success. Failure / cost: redelivery is at-least-once, requeue loops can burn capacity, a queue can become a single ordered bottleneck, and RabbitMQ is not Kafka-style retained replay by default. Set prefetch/concurrency budgets, durable or quorum queues where required, idempotent handlers and policy-managed dead lettering. Tier verdict: 1M not needed when direct calls or Kafka events suffice; 10M worth it for routed work; if selected at 100M it needs its own scaling story.

Bounded retry plus DLQ — Problem solved: recover transient delivery/dependency failures without one poison record blocking a partition or queue forever. Flow position: the consumer retries only classified transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, then parks the original payload, headers, schema version and failure reason in quarantine; an owner fixes the defect and explicitly redrives it. Failure / cost: retry amplifies outages, delayed work can violate business deadlines, and a DLQ is not automatic repair or an archive. Cap attempts and elapsed time, preserve ordering requirements, alert on oldest age/growth and reconcile before redrive. Tier verdict: 1M mandatory for any asynchronous lane; 10M mandatory; 100M needs its own scaling story for quarantine volume and operator tooling.

After-payment workers and After Payment DB — Problem solved: keep reviews, notifications, analytics and other non-critical effects off checkout latency while allowing each to lag or replay independently. Flow position: dedicated consumer groups process `PaymentCompleted`, write their own local state with an inbox/effect unique key and expose completion separately from the order's authoritative payment state. Failure / cost: users may see delayed email/review eligibility, fan-out multiplies event traffic, and one consumer's schema bug can accumulate a large backlog. Give every effect an SLO, concurrency budget, retention/rebuild plan and owner; never let its outage reject a paid order. Tier verdict: 1M worth it; 10M mandatory for failure isolation; 100M needs its own scaling story per consumer domain.

Observability and reconciliation workers — Problem solved: detect and repair ambiguous distributed state that metrics on HTTP success cannot prove correct. Flow position: traces carry checkout/order/event ids, dashboards join accepted-to-completed ratio with oldest Saga/outbox/consumer age, and scheduled reconcilers compare Checkout, Order, Inventory, Payment and PSP evidence before issuing explicit confirm/release/cancel/refund repairs. Failure / cost: high-cardinality telemetry is expensive, sampling can hide rare money errors, and an unsafe repair job can magnify corruption. Keep immutable audit evidence, dry-run repair plans and require idempotent, fenced transitions. Tier verdict: 1M mandatory; 10M mandatory; at 100M the telemetry and repair plane needs its own scaling story.

Shards and cells — Problem solved: bound dataset/restore time, write contention and regional blast radius after simpler tuning is exhausted. Flow position: a versioned router keeps Checkout, Order and Payment for one order in one cell, while Inventory remains routed by its SKU/warehouse authority; migrations copy, stream ordered changes, verify invariants, cut one range over and fence the old writer. Failure / cost: cross-cell workflows, routing-map mistakes, skew, rebalancing and duplicated platform/on-call estates are permanent complexity; independent dual writes are not a migration strategy. Tier verdict: 1M not needed; 10M not needed unless measured restore or blast-radius targets say otherwise; at 100M it needs its own scaling story and is mandatory only when those targets require it.
tradeoffs: Logical architecture versus operational estate — The picture is an excellent ownership map but an expensive day-one deployment. Keeping boxes logical at 1M preserves simple transactions and on-call; splitting the measured hot lanes at 10M buys isolation while adding network failure, versioned contracts and more deployments.

Orchestration versus choreography — Checkout Saga makes sequence, timeout and compensation visible in one place. It also becomes a control-plane hotspot and coupling point; persist state, partition workers and keep participant APIs idempotent so losing the orchestrator process loses no workflow.

Asynchronous checkout — Moving payment status and secondary effects behind the broker bounds request latency and isolates dependencies. Users now need a truthful `PENDING` contract, while operators own backlog age, replay, DLQ and workflows that can remain incomplete for hours.

Compensation is not rollback — Releasing inventory, cancelling an order or refunding a payment is a new business action that may fail after the original action became externally visible. Every compensation needs its own idempotency, legal precondition, audit record and reconciliation fallback.

Outbox guarantee — The local database change and outbox row are atomic, but publication can repeat and consumers can crash after their side effect. Stable event ids, aggregate sequence checks and inbox/effect uniqueness are permanent costs of the reliability gained.

Database per service — Ownership and failure isolation improve, but joins, reports and cross-domain consistency become asynchronous products. Do not let the Saga update another service's tables, and build analytics from events/CDC rather than cross-service request-time joins.

Adoption order — Tune query/index and pools, isolate browse from checkout, add CDN/cache and asynchronous secondary effects, then partition consumers and only later shard/cell. Each step needs a triggering metric, owner, rollback and failure drill; otherwise the architecture can only grow.

failure_review.question: Which invariant can break?
failure_review.answer: Oversell, duplicate capture and an order marked confirmed while stock or payment disagrees are the critical failures. Inventory conditional updates, one provider idempotency key and legal versioned transitions in each authoritative service guard them; the Saga coordinates but is not the source of truth for participant state.

failure_review.question: Which metric detects it first?
failure_review.answer: Watch accepted-to-completed checkout ratio and p99 together with oldest non-terminal Saga age, outbox age, consumer lag, reserve-conflict rate, PSP `UNKNOWN` age and reconciliation mismatches. Queue depth alone hides a stalled partition.

failure_review.question: How is blast radius contained?
failure_review.answer: Use separate gateway routes, pools, concurrency budgets and bounded queues for browse, cart, checkout, PSP and after-payment lanes. Partition by order/SKU as required, cap one campaign or hot SKU at admission, and let secondary consumers lag without consuming checkout capacity.

failure_review.question: Can retry duplicate or reorder work?
failure_review.answer: Yes by default. Bind the client key to a canonical request hash and original response, reuse the same provider key, assign every command/event a stable id plus aggregate version, and apply each consumer effect in a local transaction with an inbox or unique business key.

failure_review.question: How do we repair and prove recovery?
failure_review.answer: Reconcile aged Saga rows against Order, Inventory, Payment and the PSP; replay committed outboxes; repair by explicit confirm, release, cancel or refund transitions; then redrive quarantined events. Prove recovery with zero unmatched captures/reservations, bounded outbox and consumer age, and sampled aggregate sequence checks.
